ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the coordinate axes intersect at the origin O. A +Q charge is located on the left x-axis at (-r,0), a +2Q charge is located on the right x-axis at (+r,0), and a -Q charge is located on the upper y-axis at (0,+r). The distances from the three charges to the origin are all r. Reasoning: Let E0 = kQ/r^2. At the origin, the electric field produced by the left +Q is away from that positive charge, with direction +x and magnitude E0; the electric field produced by the right +2Q is away from that positive charge, with direction -x and magnitude 2E0; the electric field produced by the upper -Q points toward that negative charge, with direction +y and magnitude E0. Therefore Ex = E0 - 2E0 = -E0, Ey = E0. The magnitude of the resultant electric field is sqrt(Ex^2 + Ey^2) = sqrt((-E0)^2 + E0^2) = sqrt(2)E0 = sqrt(2)kQ/r^2.

raw_record.question_text: Three point charges of \( +Q \), \( +2Q \), and \( -Q \) are each located a distance \( r \) away from the origin, as shown above. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the origin due to these charges?

method.method_draft: Use a Cartesian component summation. From the image, identify the charges at coordinates: +Q at (-r,0), +2Q at (+r,0), and -Q at (0,+r), with the field point at the origin. From the text, use that each charge is distance r from the origin and the requested quantity is the magnitude of the net electric field. Let E0 = kQ/r^2. Determine directions at the origin: the +Q on the left gives +x field of magnitude E0; the +2Q on the right gives -x field of magnitude 2E0; the -Q above gives +y field of magnitude E0. Sum components to get Ex = E0 - 2E0 = -E0 and Ey = E0. Then compute the magnitude sqrt(Ex^2 + Ey^2) = sqrt(2)E0 = sqrt(2)kQ/r^2.

method.method_draft: Use a graphical/pairwise resultant approach. First read from the image that the two positive charges lie on the x-axis on opposite sides of the origin: +Q at left and +2Q at right, while the -Q charge is directly above the origin. From the text, all are distance r away. Compare the horizontal fields: the left +Q pushes the field at the origin to the right with magnitude kQ/r^2, while the right +2Q pushes it to the left with magnitude 2kQ/r^2, leaving a net horizontal field of kQ/r^2 to the left. Separately, the negative charge above attracts the field direction upward with magnitude kQ/r^2. These two remaining net fields are perpendicular and equal in magnitude, so the resultant is the diagonal of an equal-leg right triangle: magnitude sqrt((kQ/r^2)^2 + (kQ/r^2)^2) = sqrt(2)kQ/r^2.
